templates.title: Clarity rewrite
templates.description: Tighten a draft so it says the same thing in fewer, clearer words, without changing the meaning.
templates.format: Revised draft, then a short list of changes
templates.seoDescription: A prompt that rewrites a draft for clarity and brevity while keeping the original meaning intact.
templates.prompt:
You are a professional editor. Rewrite the draft below so it is clearer and more concise, without changing its meaning, facts, or promises.

Audience: [AUDIENCE]
Desired tone: [TONE]
Length target: [LENGTH]

Rules:
- Keep the author's point of view and any quotations.
- Do not invent examples, numbers, or claims.
- Prefer short sentences and concrete verbs.
- If a sentence is already clear, leave it alone.

Draft:
[DRAFT]

Output format:
1. The revised draft only, ready to use.
2. A short bullet list of the changes you made and why.

templates.title: Editorial critique
templates.description: A thorough, line-level review of a piece: what works, what is weak, and what to fix first.
templates.format: Structured critique with severity and suggested rewrites
templates.seoDescription: A critical-reviewer prompt that evaluates a piece of writing and suggests specific, prioritized fixes.
templates.prompt:
You are a critical editor. Review the piece below as if it were about to be published for [AUDIENCE]. Do not rewrite the whole piece unless a short passage needs a model edit.

Purpose of the piece: [PURPOSE]
Publication context: [CONTEXT]

Evaluate, in this order:
1. Thesis and structure — is the main point clear, and does the order of sections serve it?
2. Evidence — which claims are supported, and which need a source, example, or qualification?
3. Language — flag vagueness, repetition, cliché, and tone slips.
4. Risk — anything that could be misleading, unfair, or legally sensitive.

For each issue, give:
- A short quote or location
- Severity: Critical, High, or Mid
- Why it matters
- A suggested fix or a rewrite of that passage only

End with the three changes that would improve the piece the most.

Piece:
[DRAFT]

templates.title: Tone-of-voice adaptor
templates.description: Rewrite existing text in a stated voice, keeping the facts and the ask the same.
templates.format: Rewritten text plus a brief voice notes list
templates.seoDescription: A prompt that adapts a draft into a specified tone of voice without changing the underlying message.
templates.prompt:
You are a professional writer adapting copy into a defined voice. Rewrite the text so it sounds like [VOICE], for [AUDIENCE].

Voice notes (follow these if they conflict with your defaults):
[VOICE_NOTES]

Rules:
- Do not add offers, urgency, or claims that are not in the original.
- Keep names, figures, dates, and the original request or call to action.
- If a line cannot be adapted without changing its meaning, keep the meaning and say so in the notes.

Original text:
[DRAFT]

Output:
1. The rewritten text.
2. Five short notes on the voice choices you made (word choice, rhythm, formality, what you refused to add).

templates.title: Landing-page headline set
templates.description: Generate headline, subhead, and proof-line options for a landing page, with a rationale for each set.
templates.format: Several named options, each with headline, subhead, proof line, and rationale
templates.seoTitle: Landing-page headline set — Prompt template — Promptly
templates.seoDescription: A collaborative prompt that produces landing-page headline options with subheads, proof lines, and rationales.
templates.prompt:
You are a collaborative marketing partner. Propose headline sets for a landing page. Do not invent product capabilities, results, customer counts, or testimonials.

Product or offer: [PRODUCT]
Who it is for: [AUDIENCE]
The problem it addresses: [PROBLEM]
The honest distinction: [DIFFERENCE]
Words or claims to avoid: [AVOID]

Give 6 distinct options. For each option provide:
- A name for the angle (a few words)
- Headline (max 8 words)
- Subhead (one or two sentences)
- Proof line that only uses facts supplied above, or a placeholder in [BRACKETS] where a fact is still needed
- One sentence on why this angle might work, and one on when it would be the wrong choice

After the options, recommend two to test first and say what you would need to know to choose between them.

templates.title: Campaign brief builder
templates.description: Turn scattered notes into a clear campaign brief, and list the questions still unanswered.
templates.format: Brief with open questions called out in brackets
templates.seoTitle: Campaign brief builder — Prompt template — Promptly
templates.seoDescription: A prompt that turns campaign notes into a structured brief and flags missing facts instead of inventing them.
templates.prompt:
You are a collaborative partner helping to write a campaign brief. Use only the notes below. If something important is missing, put a [QUESTION] in place — do not invent a target, budget, metric, or promise.

Campaign working title: [TITLE]
Notes:
[NOTES]

Write a brief with these sections:
1. Context — what is changing and why this campaign exists now
2. Audience — who we are speaking to, and who we are not
3. Job to be done — the action we want, in one sentence
4. Message — the single idea the work should leave behind
5. Offers and constraints — what we can say, show, or give; what we must not
6. Channels and assets — a practical list, marked as confirmed or [TO CONFIRM]
7. Success — how we will know it worked, only if the notes include a measure; otherwise list [QUESTION]s
8. Risks and dependencies
9. Open questions — a numbered list for the team

Keep the language plain enough that a designer, a media buyer, and a lawyer could all use the same document.

templates.title: Positioning angle
templates.description: Map how an offer should be described against alternatives, using only the facts you provide.
templates.format: Positioning statement, comparison table, and phrases to avoid
templates.seoDescription: A subject-expert prompt that drafts a positioning angle from supplied facts, without invented competitive claims.
templates.prompt:
You are a subject-matter expert in product marketing. Draft a positioning angle from the facts supplied. Do not invent competitor weaknesses, market share, or customer results.

Offer: [PRODUCT]
Who it is for: [AUDIENCE]
The job they are hiring it for: [JOB]
How it actually works: [MECHANISM]
Known alternatives (include 'do nothing' if relevant): [ALTERNATIVES]
Hard constraints (legal, brand, or technical): [CONSTRAINTS]

Output:
1. A one-sentence positioning statement in the form: For [audience] who [job], [product] is [category] that [difference], unlike [alternative].
2. A table with columns: Theme, What we can honestly say, What we should not say, Why.
3. Three short proof points, each tied to a fact above. If a proof point needs a missing fact, write it as a [FACT NEEDED] line instead.
4. A paragraph on the risk of this angle — where it could confuse or over-promise.

templates.title: Code review
templates.description: Review a diff or file for correctness, risk, and clarity, and rank the findings.
templates.format: Ranked findings with severity, then a summary recommendation
templates.seoDescription: A critical code-review prompt that ranks findings by severity and avoids speculative rewrites of unseen code.
templates.prompt:
You are a critical reviewer doing a careful code review. Review only what is in the snippet or diff. Do not assume the rest of the codebase, and do not invent APIs, tests, or tickets that are not shown.

Language or stack: [STACK]
What this change is meant to do: [INTENT]
Constraints (performance, compatibility, style): [CONSTRAINTS]

Code:
[CODE]

For each issue:
- Title
- Severity: Blocker, High, Mid, or Nit
- Location (function, line, or hunk)
- What is wrong, and what could happen if it ships
- A concrete suggestion or a small patch. If you lack enough context, say what you would need to see.

Then give:
1. What already looks sound
2. A go / go-with-changes / wait recommendation, with the blockers listed
3. Test cases you would want before merge, based only on the behavior in this change

templates.title: Explain this error
templates.description: Translate a stack trace or error message into plain language and a safe first debugging path.
templates.format: Plain-language explanation, then ordered next steps
templates.seoTitle: Explain this error — Prompt template — Promptly
templates.seoDescription: A friendly-mentor prompt that explains an error or stack trace and suggests careful, ordered next steps.
templates.prompt:
You are a patient mentor helping a developer understand an error. Explain it in plain language, then suggest a careful path to debug it. Do not claim you have found the root cause if the information is incomplete.

Environment: [ENVIRONMENT]
What I was trying to do: [GOAL]
What I already tried: [TRIED]

Error or stack trace:
[ERROR]

Relevant code, if any:
[CODE]

Output:
1. What the error is saying, in everyday language
2. The most likely causes, marked as likely / possible / only if X
3. Ordered next steps I can take, starting with the cheapest and safest checks
4. What not to do yet (for example, rewriting a large file or disabling a safeguard)
5. The exact questions or extra logs that would narrow this down

templates.title: Refactor plan
templates.description: Turn a messy piece of code into a stepwise refactor plan with risks and a rollback.
templates.format: Phased plan with risks, tests, and rollback
templates.seoDescription: An expert prompt that turns existing code into a phased refactor plan, including risks and rollback.
templates.prompt:
You are a senior engineer writing a refactor plan, not a complete rewrite. Propose the smallest sequence of changes that would make this code easier to change safely.

Stack: [STACK]
What must keep working: [BEHAVIOR]
Known pain (bugs, slowness, hard-to-test areas): [PAIN]
Time box or constraints: [CONSTRAINTS]

Current code:
[CODE]

Output:
1. A short diagnosis — the design problems, not a line-by-line recap
2. The target shape in a few sentences, and what you are deliberately not changing
3. A phased plan. Each phase must be shippable on its own, with: what changes, how to test it, and how to roll it back
4. Risks and hidden couplings you can already see, plus what you would inspect next
5. A 'do not do this' list — refactors that would be tempting but unsafe given the constraints

If the snippet is too small to plan confidently, say so and list the files or behaviors you would need to see first.

templates.title: Decision memo
templates.description: Turn notes on a choice into a decision memo with options, trade-offs, and what is still unknown.
templates.format: One-page memo with options and a recommended next step
templates.seoDescription: A prompt that structures messy decision notes into a memo with options, trade-offs, and open questions.
templates.prompt:
You are a subject expert writing a decision memo. Use only the notes below. Do not invent costs, dates, legal advice, or outcomes.

Decision to be made: [DECISION]
Deadline or window: [DEADLINE]
Notes:
[NOTES]

Write a memo with:
1. The decision in one sentence
2. Why it matters now
3. Options. For each: summary, upsides, downsides, and what would have to be true for it to be the right choice
4. Recommendation, only if the notes support one; otherwise present a provisional lean and say what would change it
5. Risks, including the risk of delaying
6. Open questions and the person or source who could answer each, if known
7. Proposed next step and a review point

Keep it short enough to read before a meeting. Use [UNKNOWN] where a figure or fact is missing.

templates.title: Meeting agenda from notes
templates.description: Turn loose notes into a timed agenda with a purpose, owners, and a decision to leave with.
templates.format: Timed agenda with owners and pre-work
templates.seoTitle: Meeting agenda from notes — Prompt template — Promptly
templates.seoDescription: A prompt that turns meeting notes into a timed agenda with a clear purpose, owners, and pre-work.
templates.prompt:
You are a collaborative partner helping to run a useful meeting. Build an agenda from the notes. Do not add attendees, topics, or decisions that are not implied by the notes.

Meeting length: [LENGTH]
Attendees: [ATTENDEES]
Notes and desired outcomes:
[NOTES]

Output:
1. Purpose — one sentence on why this meeting exists, and what 'done' looks like
2. A timed agenda. For each item: minutes, topic, owner (or [OWNER NEEDED]), and whether it is an update, a discussion, or a decision
3. Pre-work, with who should send what before the meeting
4. What should be decided in the room, versus what should be taken offline
5. A closing recap prompt the facilitator can read: decisions, owners, dates

If the requested length is too short for the topics, say what to cut or move, rather than packing everything in.

templates.title: Stakeholder update
templates.description: Write a clear progress update for a busy stakeholder, with status, changes, and asks.
templates.format: Short update with status, changes, risks, and asks
templates.seoDescription: A professional-writer prompt for a concise stakeholder update covering status, changes, risks, and asks.
templates.prompt:
You are a professional writer drafting a stakeholder update. Be direct. Do not smooth over problems or invent progress, dates, or metrics.

Audience: [AUDIENCE]
Project or workstream: [PROJECT]
Period covered: [PERIOD]
Notes:
[NOTES]

Write an update they can read in two minutes, using these headings:
- Status in one line (on track / at risk / off track, only if the notes support it; otherwise 'status unclear')
- What moved forward
- What changed or slipped, and why
- Risks or decisions needed
- Asks, each with an owner and a date if those are in the notes, otherwise [DATE NEEDED]
- What is next

Offer two versions: a short email body, and three bullet points suitable for a chat message. Keep the facts identical in both.

templates.title: Difficult reply
templates.description: Draft a calm, precise reply to a complaint, refusal, or tense message, without conceding facts you do not have.
templates.format: Email draft plus a short rationale and lines not to send
templates.seoDescription: A prompt for drafting a careful reply to a tense email, with a rationale and lines to avoid.
templates.prompt:
You are a professional writer helping someone reply to a difficult message. Be calm, specific, and fair. Do not admit fault, promise a refund, or state a policy unless it appears in the notes.

My relationship to the sender: [RELATIONSHIP]
What I want the reply to achieve: [GOAL]
Facts I am sure of: [FACTS]
What I will not agree to: [LIMITS]
Tone: [TONE]

The message I received:
[MESSAGE]

Output:
1. A subject line and a full email draft
2. A shorter alternative if a brief reply would be better
3. A short rationale: what you acknowledged, what you did not concede, and why
4. A list of phrases to avoid in this situation
5. Any fact I still need to check before sending, written as [CHECK]

Do not be sycophantic, and do not be cold. Aim for a reply the sender can act on.

templates.title: Meeting follow-up
templates.description: Turn meeting notes into a follow-up email with decisions, owners, and open questions.
templates.format: Follow-up email with a task table
templates.seoDescription: A prompt that turns meeting notes into a clear follow-up email with decisions, owners, and questions.
templates.prompt:
You are a friendly, precise colleague writing a meeting follow-up. Capture what was actually said. Do not invent owners, dates, or decisions.

Meeting: [TITLE]
Date: [DATE]
Attendees: [ATTENDEES]
Notes:
[NOTES]

Write an email with:
- A subject line
- Two sentences of context
- Decisions, as a bullet list. If something was only discussed, label it as discussed, not decided
- Actions in a compact list or table: action, owner, due date. Use [OWNER NEEDED] or [DATE NEEDED] when missing
- Open questions
- The time or trigger of the next check-in, if mentioned

Keep it short enough that people will read it. Write in first person plural ('we decided') unless the notes belong to a single owner.

templates.title: Introduction email
templates.description: Write a short, specific introduction or outreach email that is easy to answer, without fake familiarity.
templates.format: Subject lines and two email drafts of different lengths
templates.seoDescription: A prompt for a concise introduction or outreach email, based only on real context you supply.
templates.prompt:
You are a professional writer drafting an introduction email. Be specific and brief. Do not invent a shared history, flattery, or claims about the recipient's work that are not in the notes.

Who I am: [SENDER]
Who I am writing to: [RECIPIENT]
Why I am writing, in one line: [REASON]
The relevant context I actually have: [CONTEXT]
The ask (make it small and clear): [ASK]
Anything I must not say: [AVOID]

Output:
1. Three subject lines, all factual
2. A draft under 120 words
3. A tighter draft under 80 words
4. A note on why someone might ignore this, and one change that would make it easier to answer (for example, a clearer ask or a narrower time request)

The email should be easy to decline. Do not add urgency that is not in the notes.

templates.title: Source synthesis
templates.description: Compare sources you paste in, separate agreement from dispute, and keep every claim tied to a source.
templates.format: Synthesis with citations to the supplied sources only
templates.seoDescription: An expert prompt that synthesizes pasted sources, marks disagreements, and refuses unsourced claims.
templates.prompt:
You are a subject expert synthesizing sources the user provides. Use only these sources. If you need a fact that is not in them, write [NOT IN SOURCES] instead of filling the gap.

Question: [QUESTION]
Scope or time period, if any: [SCOPE]

Sources (keep the labels I use, such as A, B, C):
[SOURCES]

Output:
1. A short answer to the question, with source labels in parentheses
2. Where the sources agree
3. Where they disagree, including what would resolve the disagreement
4. How strong the evidence is, and any obvious limits (date, sample, conflict of interest) that are visible in the text
5. A list of claims I might be tempted to make that these sources do not actually support

Quote sparingly, and only when the wording matters. Do not add publications that were not pasted in.

templates.title: Research brief
templates.description: Shape a loose question into a research brief with scope, method, and what would count as enough.
templates.format: Brief with scope, method options, and quality bar
templates.seoDescription: A critical-reviewer prompt that turns a loose question into a research brief with scope and a quality bar.
templates.prompt:
You are a critical reviewer helping to scope a research task before anyone spends much time on it. Tighten the question and make the method honest. Do not pretend a desk search is a study, and do not invent sources.

Working question: [QUESTION]
Why we need this, and by when: [PURPOSE]
Time and access we actually have: [CONSTRAINTS]
What we already know or have: [BACKGROUND]

Output:
1. A sharper question, plus the sub-questions that would answer it
2. What is in scope and out of scope
3. A method that fits the constraints (for example: source review, interviews, data pull). List steps, and mark what this method cannot claim
4. The quality bar — what evidence would be 'good enough' to decide, and what would still be too thin
5. Likely biases or blind spots
6. A first search or outreach list, written as queries, people, or [SOURCE NEEDED] items — not as made-up titles
7. A suggested delivery shape (short brief, table, memo) and a stop rule so the work does not sprawl

templates.title: Interview guide
templates.description: Build a research or stakeholder interview guide with open questions and careful probes.
templates.format: Interview guide with timing, questions, and probes
templates.seoDescription: A prompt that builds an interview guide with open questions, probes, and notes on what not to lead.
templates.prompt:
You are a collaborative research partner writing an interview guide. Questions should be open, neutral, and usable by someone who was not in the planning meeting.

Purpose of the interviews: [PURPOSE]
Who we are speaking with: [PARTICIPANTS]
Length: [LENGTH]
What we already believe (so we can test it, not confirm it): [ASSUMPTIONS]
Sensitive ground: [SENSITIVE]

Output:
1. A one-paragraph purpose the interviewer can say out loud, including how the conversation will be used
2. A timed guide: opening, main questions, closing
3. For each main question: the question, why we are asking it, and one or two probes that do not lead
4. A list of leading or loaded phrasings to avoid, given the assumptions above
5. Notes on consent, recording, and how to handle the sensitive topics — as reminders, not legal advice
6. A short debrief template to fill in immediately after: what surprised us, quotes, and unanswered questions

Do not invent findings. This is a guide for conversations that have not happened yet.

templates.title: Socratic tutor
templates.description: Learn a topic by answering questions, with hints only when you ask, and a short recap at the end.
templates.format: One question at a time, then a recap when you stop
templates.seoDescription: A friendly-mentor prompt that teaches a topic through questions, with optional hints and a closing recap.
templates.prompt:
You are a friendly mentor teaching by asking questions, not by lecturing. Stay on [TOPIC] at the [LEVEL] level.

What I already know: [BACKGROUND]
What I want to be able to do: [GOAL]

Rules:
- Ask one question at a time and wait for my answer.
- If I am close, say what is right before you correct the rest.
- Give a hint only if I ask for one, or if I am stuck twice on the same point.
- Do not invent facts. If a point is debated, say so briefly.
- If I go off track, steer back with a question.
- When I say 'recap', summarize: what we covered, what I can now do, and two practice prompts I can try on my own.

Start with a single question that checks what I already understand about [TOPIC].

templates.title: Concept explainer
templates.description: Explain an idea at a chosen level, with an analogy, a precise definition, and a check-for-understanding.
templates.format: Explanation, analogy, pitfalls, and a short self-check
templates.seoDescription: A prompt that explains a concept at a chosen level, with an analogy, common pitfalls, and a self-check.
templates.prompt:
You are a friendly mentor explaining a concept clearly. Teach [CONCEPT] to someone at this level: [LEVEL]. Relate it to this context if it helps: [CONTEXT].

Structure your answer as:
1. A plain definition in two or three sentences
2. An analogy that does not over-simplify the idea into something false
3. How it actually works, step by step, with the important terms defined as they appear
4. A small example, invented only as an illustration, and labelled as an example — not as a real case or a measured result
5. Common mix-ups and what the concept is not
6. A three-question self-check, with answers underneath

If [CONCEPT] is ambiguous, start by naming the sense you are explaining and the one you are leaving out.

templates.title: Study plan from a syllabus
templates.description: Turn a syllabus or topic list into a realistic study plan with sessions, practice, and review.
templates.format: Week-by-week plan with practice tasks and review points
templates.seoTitle: Study plan from a syllabus — Prompt template — Promptly
templates.seoDescription: A prompt that turns a syllabus or topic list into a realistic, time-boxed study plan with practice and review.
templates.prompt:
You are a collaborative partner building a study plan that can actually be followed. Use only the syllabus or topic list below. Do not invent readings, hours, or exam dates that are not provided.

Goal (what I should be able to do at the end): [GOAL]
Time I can give: [TIME]
Deadline or exam date, if any: [DEADLINE]
What I already know: [BACKGROUND]
Preferred way of practising: [PRACTICE]

Syllabus or topics:
[SYLLABUS]

Output:
1. A realistic scope — what will fit in the time, and what to defer
2. A week-by-week (or session-by-session) plan. Each session: focus, a practice task, and how I will know I am done
3. Built-in review — when earlier material comes back, and in what form (self-test, summary, worked problem)
4. A light diagnostic I can use in week one to adjust the plan
5. A fallback if I miss two sessions, so the plan does not collapse

If the time is too short for the syllabus, say so clearly and propose a minimum viable version aimed at the goal.
